#1783. ‘Not ready’, ‘out of control’ and ‘the end of the world’: What Amorim’s words tell us about Milan’s state

Ruben Amorim is not one to hold back when it comes to speaking his thoughts to the media, and the last few days are no exception.

The past week or so has seen Amorim have to digest the best and worst of his AC Milan side. The 3-1 derby win over Inter generated a euphoria that begun whispers of the word ‘Scudetto’, before a dismal defeat to Ferencvaros which saw Milan drop to 29th in the Europa League standings.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

This rollercoaster of extremes didn’t stop either side of those two games either. Before the victory over the Nerazzurri a 2-1 lead had been coughed up against Bologna, who scored three times in the second half to win at San Siro and inflict the first league defeat on the Rossoneri.

Yesterday, the Diavolo responded to the season low-point against the Hungarians by beating a Genoa side that had won their last three games and four of their last five. This Milan team is a very difficult one to work out, and it seems even the manager is struggling to do so.

After the Ferencvaros and Genoa games, we learned a lot about where Amorim sees his team to be at. Some key lines from his post-match comments demonstrated a wide spectrum of reaction, from anger to pride, passing through encouragement and worry.

Ruben Amorim has often gone to bat for his players after negative performances and results this season, but it seems that the defeat on Thursday night had pushed his patience to the brink as he tore into his team after the game.

“There’s no explanation. There’s nothing I can say, especially about the first half. I don’t remember another first half like it. It’s about ambition, concentration, desire,” he said.

“We gave away opportunities, we gave away stupid gifts. We weren’t prepared to play football tonight. I usually have a lot to say in defence of our team, but not tonight. We need to be more humble and understand what happened.”

For the first time we saw a peek behind the mask, one that has very often been one portraying an optimistic and positive expression. Amorim knew there was no point attempting to lie to the supporters, the media but above all to himself.

What we know is that Amorim echoed the ferocity of these sentiments when speaking in the dressing room after full-time in what was likely the first dressing down that the team got. Six players were reported to have disappointed more than the others, too.

Above all, what stood out was the fact that the head coach opted to question whether his players wanted it enough. This was no longer a question of learning an identity, rotation or an injury crisis: it became a matter of heart.

Another intriguing extract from the post-Ferencvaros tirade that Amorim went on was about the squad’s ability to balance playing in two different competitions, namely Serie A and the Europa League.

“We’re not ready to be competitive on two fronts. We need to work on our way of looking at football and how we approach matches. There are no excuses tonight, there’s nothing I can say.

“I have to focus on the league, obviously, but we also have to do well in the Europa League. We must and can win games despite the rotation. We have to be ready – we’re not now – to play and win every three days.

“But I won’t give up on this competition. But as long as the mathematics don’t condemn us, we’ll fight in this competition as we do in the others.”

Once again, Amorim offered a bit of a revelation: the league is the absolute priority for Milan this season. It may not exactly be revolutionary information, given that a top four spot remains the most accessible avenue to the main objective for 2026-27: securing a Champions League return.

And yet, in his emotional outburst, the former Sporting CP and Manchester United boss told us all in black and white that Serie A will be the focus. As a result, it’s right to expect more ups and downs in Europe, especially with such a depleted squad.

There is an element of observational realism about Amorim’s words; almost an admission of defeat in his attempts to spin two plates at the same time and get the most out of the resources at his disposal. Does it suggest a Europa League resurgence is coming? Not exactly.

Amorim has not made a habit of mentioning individuals ever since his arrivals, both in his pre-match words but especially after games in which emotions are running high. However, he brought up someone who was absent for the Ferencvaros game.

“Everyone needs to train like Pavlovic. He’s ready to die in training. He’s a good example. Sometimes when players don’t start, they struggle. But there are no excuses, we should have won even with those who started,” he said.

Going into the season there were some who were legitimately questioning whether Strahinja Pavlovic would even be a tactical fit for Amorim’s usual 3-4-2-1 system, given that he prefers more composed, ball-playing outside centre-backs.

The answer to those doubts is that in November the Serbian has become the shining light in the eyes of his manager. We mentioned earlier that it had become a question of heart, and nobody can doubt that Pavlovic has that in abundance.

For all of the talk about tactics, systems, shapes and patterns, football is a simple game that very often comes down to who wants it more. In this regard, Amorim elevated Pavlovic as the example to follow, while hoping he returns from injury for the Frosinone game after the break.

Moving on to the post-Genoa reflections, what was quite apparent was that Ruben Amorim was in no mood to get carried away. In fact, if anything, he revealed his belief that his team are still miles off where he wants them.

“What I feel is that, when we’re competitive, we’re difficult to beat, and now we’re steering the game towards our style. We push for control with the ball.

“When we’re not able to be competitive, we’re completely out of control. It’s a big difference, but it’s something we need to work on. But again, the team’s evolution, the way we’re playing, is completely different from the start of the season, and I’m happy with that.

“We should have more points. I’m clearly not happy with the European games, not just because of the results, but because of the performance. Results can happen, but the performances are far from what we want. However, I think we’ll be a better team in the future.”

So, for now this version of Milan is not one that satisfies the coach. The words are a good summary of what the last six games have shown, in which there have been an even split of victories and defeats: on their day the team can beat anyone in the league, but on an off-day they can lose to anyone too.

What Amorim seems keen to hammer home is that progress for this season will be judged on the ability to bring the ceiling closer to the floor. In other words, we have seen the potential of this team already with some impressive wins, yet the base level for performances remains frighteningly low.

Consistency is not just about being able to string together several positive results in a row, something the current Rossoneri do not seem capable of. It is about the repeated displaying of an idea and an identity every few days, to suggest the team are getting closer to the vision the coach has.

Various things make that difficult (perhaps unachievable, based on Amorim’s other comments) right now, such as the injury situation and the multiple windows needed to sculpt the squad. Progress is not always linear, but the target has been set.

One of the themes that Amorim has been consistently questioned on this season is how to unlock the club-record signing Goncalo Ramos, who remains stuck on three goals (one of which was a penalty).

After the Genoa game, he said: “I think we’re lacking time in the final third. We control the ball away from the opponent’s penalty area. This is also key for Goncalo Ramos to have more clear-cut chances. It’s clearly not Goncalo’s fault.

“Pulisic is far from the penalty area. Gonçalo is far from the penalty area. All these players play away from the penalty area, so I can say we’re still far from the final product, because we’re still working on good progression, but then in the final third of the pitch we waste a lot of time with the ball there.”

This is one of the points of ‘evolution’ that Amorim clearly wants to see from his side, but is yet to achieve. Milan are not yet a team that can sustain pressure in the opposition half, nor can they penetrate the box with any regularity either.

In fact, a report from Sky backed this up with some interesting numbers, look specifically at data per 30 minutes of actual possession. Milan are first in Serie A for build-up actions, but they are 20th for entries into the final third and entries into the opposition box.

Amorim’s side are 19th for percentage of touches in the attacking third and 18th in percentage of touches in the opposition box. When the Rossoneri have the ball, it is rarely in a threatening area.

With numbers like these, there isn’t much for Ramos to get on the end of, and it makes the positive attacking numbers (23 goals in 11 league games) feel quite unsustainable.

The Portuguese striker meanwhile is first in the Milan squad in Serie A for interceptions, recoveries, touches in the middle third and touches in the opposition half. He is second for receptions, touches and duels, and third for passes.

Simply put, the No.9 is being drawn away from the area he should be operating in because the team are not capable of sustaining spells of possession further up the field, so he needs to drop deeper to feel involved.

This is something Amorim must work on, because while the goals are coming from other sources for now – in some cases due to the space Ramos helps create – it could all come tumbling down unless the attacking play improves more generally.

🚨🎙️🛡️ Ruben Amorim on Gonçalo Ramos: “Ramos is helping US more than we are helping him. It’s a TEAM problem, not a Ramos problem.”

“We don’t spend enough time in the final third.”

“When we start keeping the ball there more often, Gonçalo is going to score MANY goals.” pic.twitter.com/b3Zs6YxNym

— Milan Wire (@MilanWireX) November 8, 2026

Finally, we end with what was perhaps the most passionate part of Amorim’s comments following the win at the Stadio Luigi Ferraris on Sunday, again centred around the levels he expects from his team.

“It’s the mentality. When you’re a player, there are no off days. If you play for Milan, for these clubs, there are no off days. You can’t show up like we did on Thursday and then turn it on again for Sunday. It’s not possible, it’s not something that will work.

“It’s not a physical condition, it’s a question of anxiety about defeat. If you ‘panic’ about defeat, it’s not that you’re afraid of losing, but that you know that losing is the end of the world. That’s the feeling I want my teams to have.”

In many ways, the manager was speaking in a way that channels how fans have experienced the past week. How is it possible that Milan can be completely outplayed by a side sat third in the Hungarian lead just days after convincingly beating the Italian champions?

Against Genoa, how can the team play as they did in the first half, and then appear to completely drop off a cliff in the second half when the time came to dig deep and bring the result home? The disparity in levels both in-game and from match to match is astounding everyone, even the man in charge.

What Amorim said about wanting his side to fear losing was particularly poignant. In his time at the club so far he has repeatedly stressed that feeling of responsibility to honour the red and black shirt and all that comes with that, including the importance of results.

Some may argue that encouraging an ‘end of the world’ type mentality will not help the players play more carefree and will actually only stiffen them up. Yet, it could also provide the stimulus for the fight and the courage that Amorim clearly so desperately wants.

There is a hint of irony about the ‘no days off’ comment, as Amorim has given the squad a one-week break, at least those who were not called up by their national teams. When everyone reconvenes there will be another crucial stretch of games to see out the year, starting with a home match against the surprise package Frosinone.

For all of the energy, passion and emotion that Ruben Amorim speaks with, it will eventually be time for words to become deeds. Consistency must be not a distant mirage but some thing tangible that emerges.

Only then will a full buy-in be achieved and patience be awarded. Otherwise there will always be the fear that darkness follows light.

#1782. Mauricio Pochettino to Man United: Five signings the Red Devils could make in 2027 to transform themselves under Argentine

By Matt Law | 11 Nov 2026 18:13, Last updated: 11 Nov 2026 18:18

Manchester United are soon expected to confirm Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach, with Michael Carrick set to be relieved of his duties at Old Trafford.

An announcement from Man United on the removal of Carrick is likely to arrive on Thursday, with Pochettino leaving his managerial role with the United States in order to take charge of the 20-time English champions.

Man United are expected to at least attempt to add to their squad in January, but the bulk of their business for 2027 will have to wait until the summer.

Here, Sports Mole looks at five signings the Red Devils could make in the middle of next year to hand Pochettino a huge chance of enjoying a successful 2027-28 campaign.

Man United overhauled their midfield during the summer transfer window, bringing in Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, but it would be fair to say that the balance in the middle of the park is still not quite right at this moment in time.

Manuel Ugarte is likely to leave next summer, once he has recovered from a serious knee injury, while there are question marks surrounding Bruno Fernandes' long-term future.

As a result, there is expected to be space in the squad for another midfield arrival, and bringing in Scott from Bournemouth would be a huge statement of intent.

The 23-year-old - valued in the region of £80m by Bournemouth - is also wanted by Chelsea, Arsenal and Liverpool.

However, Man United should also be firmly in the mix for the England international, who has quickly developed into one of the leading central midfielders in the Premier League.

There is currently widespread speculation surrounding Karl's future at Bayern, with the Germany international potentially being allowed to leave Allianz Arena in 2027.

Karl, 18, has scored three goals and registered two assists in 14 appearances for Vincent Kompany's side during the 2026-27 campaign.

The versatile attacker has represented Bayern on 54 occasions, scoring 12 goals and registering 10 assists, and a recent report claimed that Man United had been 'alerted' to the possibility that the teenager could be available in 2027.

Karl is said to be valued by Bayern in the region of £50m, and he could potentially be a long-term replacement for Fernandes at Old Trafford.

There is currently a host of speculation surrounding Esposito's future, with Arsenal and Man United believed to be interested in the Italy international.

The 21-year-old has scored four times in 13 appearances for Inter this season, in addition to coming up with two assists, while he has 15 goals and nine assists in 63 appearances for the club in total since breaking into the first team.

The 6ft 3in striker is said to be valued by Inter in the region of £84m, so it would be a major deal for Man United.

Benjamin Sesko's ongoing injury problems are a concern, and it would be some statement from the Red Devils if they were able to win the race for Esposito, who was allegedly scouted by the English giants last weekend.

Man United are long-term admirers of Branthwaite, with the Red Devils making an attempt to sign the centre-back from Everton in the summer of 2024.

It is understood that the Red Devils had at least two offers for the Englishman turned down, but it is possible that their interest could be reignited in 2027.

Branthwaite has made nine appearances for Everton this season, and the 24-year-old is producing high-level performances for the Merseyside outfit.

The Englishman has a contract with Everton until the summer of 2030, but it would be difficult for the Toffees to fight off serious interest from Man United next year.

Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez are both likely to leave Old Trafford in 2027, and it is absolutely vital that the Red Devils boost their defence next summer.

Man United attempted to sign Hall from Newcastle over the summer, but the club were ultimately unable to secure a deal for the England international.

The 22-year-old signed a new contract with the Magpies in September, with his contract at St James' Park due to run until the summer of 2031.

However, it is not impossible to imagine Hall being on the move next summer, with Man United desperate to bring in a new left-back.

Luke Shaw could be released next summer, and Man United need a long-term option in that area of the field, with Hall said to be incredibly keen on a switch to Old Trafford.

#1781. Marco Rose's Bournemouth should not have the depth to win this many games domestically and abroad but at Ipswich they showed they can do it the hard way, writes JAMES SHARPE

Published: 11:20 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 12:48 EST, 8 November 2026

Juggling domestic duties with European adventures should not be as manageable as this for teams like Bournemouth.

Clubs of their size should be creaking under the weight of the extra fixtures. All those games, all that travelling. They have played nine games in a month.

Far bigger outfits have toiled spinning those plates. Remember when Ange Postecoglou stopped bothering about the Premier League entirely just to focus on the Europa League.

And yet here are those brilliant Cherries, three days after a win in Prague in that same competition, making it eight on the bounce with a victory at Ipswich thanks to Evanilson's opener, following goalkeeper Christian Walton's early howler, and an own goal from Leif Davis.

Bournemouth haven't done that since 2013 when they were getting out of League One.

Now, they are seventh in the Premier League, second in the Europa League.

Leif Davies reacts after scoring an own goal to make it 2-0 to Bournemouth

And they're in the League Cup quarter-finals – all while having the squad depth to name Alex Scott and Junior Kroupi on the bench.

Marco Rose's side showed they can also do it the hard way, too, after Jack Clarke's second-half penalty for Ipswich, given for a soft foul on Abdoul Ouattara, provided a far more tense final 15 minutes than anticipated inside a feverish Portman Road where Julio Enciso also twice went close from late free-kicks.

'One goal changed the momentum of the game and that's why I'm much more pleased about the last 20 minutes because we suffered but we did it together,' said Rose.

First James Trafford, now Walton. Bournemouth's win over Leeds last weekend also hinged on a goalkeeping howler, when Trafford's simple pass out from the back was intercepted.

This time Ipswich stalwart Walton took a back pass from Dara O'Shea and decided the best course of action was to try to dummy and turn Evanilson. He failed, of course.

Evanilson rolled the ball into an empty net. That intense Bournemouth press really can do some crazy things to you.

IPSWICH (4-2-3-1): Walton 4; Ouattara 5, Diop 6, O'Shea 6, Davis 5; Florentino 7 (Akpom 85), Palacios 6; Maeda 6 (Fatawu 65, 7), Enciso 7; Philogene 6 (Clarke 54, 7); Emersonn 5 (Flemming 54, 6)

BOURNEMOUTH (4-2-3-1): Petrovic 6; Smith 6 (Diakite 79), Hill 7, Silva 7; Truffert 7; Adams 7, Christie 6 (Cook 67, 5); Rayan 6 (Adli 86), Kluivert 6 (Kroupi 68, 6), Tavernier 7; EVANILSON 8 (Rodriguez 85)

After scoring the opener in Bournemouth's win last weekend, manager Marco Rose told Evanilson that he was becoming a 'real No9'.

That's six goals now in his last seven games but it's his all-round play that's so impressive.

He dropped in and played a beautiful curling through ball into the channel to set Justin Kluivert free down the right.

He collected the loose ball for the second goal.

He made a fine run to latch on to a free-kick over the defence to stab the ball over to James Hill at the back post, who headed over from close range, which would have put him level with Declan Rice as the leading assister in the league too.

'He's so hard-working,' added Rose. 'He does everything out of possession.

'He starts the press, he plays in between the lines, he gives us deep runs.

'But the most important thing is scoring and he understood that he also needs to arrive close to goal if he wants to score.'

If the Tractor Boys are to make their stay in the Premier League a longer one than last time, they cannot afford to keep giving early leads. The mountain is steep enough.

Evanilson's opener was the sixth time Ipswich have conceded inside the first 15 minutes of a league game this season. They are yet to score one that early.

A howler from Ipswich keeper Christian Walton gifted Evanilson the opener

James Hill celebrates Bournemouth's win which lifts them to seventh

It is what will make this defeat especially frustrating for Gary O'Neil against his former club. 'Gary, what's the score?' chimed the travelling fans.

For so much of the contest, Ipswich looked composed and confident on the ball, played with energy and intent and, after they pulled one back, showed how much pressure they can put teams under and how much this place can bounce.

They are a much better side than the one that came up last time but you cannot come out after the break and have Ouattara give the ball straight to Evanilson again inside 30 seconds as he did before Ryan Christie's shot took two deflections and went in.

'Gutted,' said O'Neil. 'To lose a game that you haven't been outclassed is tough to take. We restricted Bournemouth to nothing of their own doing. If you give the ball to the opposition number nine twice, it's going to be difficult.'

#1780. Andorra vs Gibraltar - prediction, team news, lineups

By Lewis Nolan | 11 Nov 2026 18:15

Andorra will conclude their Nations League D campaign on Friday, when they welcome Gibraltar to Estadi de la FAF d'Encamp.

The hosts are last in their three-team group with one point from their three matches so far, whereas the visitors are second with two points from two games.

Andorra were beaten 1-0 by Malta on October 4 in their latest outing in the competition, with their only point coming in a 0-0 stalemate with Gibraltar on September 27.

All three teams in their group will be competing in Nations League C in 2028-29, but while there is no jeopardy for either team on Friday, their placement in group will determine their rankings for the next campaign.

The hosts have only scored one goal in the group so far, though they have conceded just three times in the group stage.

Boss Koldo Alvarez has been in charge of the national team for 16 years, but he has only overseen 13 wins from his 146 games in the dugout, and he has lost 15, drawn five and won just one of his last 21 matches as head coach.

Andorra's performances at home have been poor considering they have been beaten in six of their past seven fixtures when playing as hosts.

Gibraltar are in arguably their best ever period of form given they are undefeated in their last six fixtures in all competitions, winning on three occasions.

The visitors managed to score 11 goals and concede just twice, and they kept four clean sheets in that time.

It should be noted that Los Llanis did play Liechtenstein, Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands and Sao Tome and Principe in those six clashes, with the latter the highest-ranked nation by FIFA at 194th.

Head coach Scott Wiseman will hope to avoid becoming the first manager in his country's history to lose against Andorra, with his side having won two times and settled for two stalemates in four meetings with their hosts.

Gibraltar have been defeated in five of their seven most recent contests on the road, with their only victory in that period a 2-0 success against Liechtenstein on October 5.

Andorra could use a four-man defence featuring central defenders Max Llovera and Ian Bryan Olivera ahead of goalkeeper Iker Alvarez.

Midfielders Ot Remolins Planes and Eric Vales could be rewarded with their 11th and 25th caps for the national team.

In the frontline, it would not be surprising to see forward Albert Rosas partnered by Guillaume Lopez, with the duo having scored five and two goals respectively for the hosts.

As for Gibraltar, it would not be surprising to see Dan Bent, Bernardo Lopes and Julian Valarino form a back three, especially after the trio started in the reverse fixture against their hosts.

Leon Mason and Nicholas Pozo may be used as two third of a midfield three, while Tjay De Barr and Dylan Borge are set to start up front.

Alvarez; Font, Llovera, Olivera, Nicolas; Alaez, Planes, Vales, Rodrigo; Rosas, Lopez

Banda; Bent, Lopes, Valarino; Ronan, Mason, Torrilla, Pozo, Scanlon; De Barr, Borge

Neither side are likely to be at their best considering there is little to play for given all teams will be in Nations League C.

However, with Andorra backed by a home crowd, perhaps the hosts will be able take at least a point against Gibraltar, who have often travelled poorly.

#1779. GdS: Milan ready €50m January assault for Tresoldi to give Ramos a partner – the strategy

AC Milan are serious about signing Nicolo Tresoldi from Club Brugge, with an attempt being readied ahead of the winter window.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, Milan intend to sign another striker even before the summer arrives, in order to boost their Champions League hopes. The name that they have chosen is someone the fans already know well: Nicolo Tresoldi.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

At the end of June, the club announced the signing of Gonçalo Ramos for over €70m, the most expensive signing in the club’s history to date (and likely for a while to come). Ramos hasn’t – at least for now – cured Milan’s goal-scoring deficiency in the No.9 role.

The negotiations for Tresoldi, however, are shaping up to be costly. Last summer, Club Brugge rejected another Italian offer of €35m from Roma, and in the meantime the price has skyrocketed after the forward bagged 13 goals in 15 games.

Adding his four goals this season against Germany’s youth team brings him close to 20 for the season already. His league hat-trick against VV Sint-Truiden at the end of October followed his hat-trick at San Siro against Inter, marking the night that every Rossoneri fan knew his name.

Therefore, the cost could now be around €50m, another huge expense if Milan really decide to go all-in. The club made a €24m loss in the last accounts after three years of profit, and the temptation is to speculate to accumulate, i.e. to invest more and make sure of the Champions League revenues.

There’s a desire to finalise the deal as early as the January transfer window, unless Brugge move to raise the price, perhaps due to a potential foreign competition. Milan believe that their relationship with the Belgian side is actually strong, with Gerry Cardinale ready to lead talks again.

As for Ramos, the investment so far has yielded just three goals and two assists, which doesn’t mean he wasn’t effective and is ready to be shelved, but it’s precisely when paired with another striker that the management believes the Portuguese could be more productive.

In short, a two-striker team can’t be ruled out in the future, with Tresoldi alongside the former Benfica man. In the European race goals fuel the climb, and Milan know this after last season’s late collapse, keen to avoid it again.

Should Milan hit a wall erected by Club Brugge, they would leave the Tresoldi option open for the summer. In the meantime, they would fill the gap with a striker on loan from a top European club.

However, Tresoldi could provide an initial assist for Milan: his support for the Rossoneri is well-known and has been publicly stated, so among the various options available, Nicolò would choose the San Siro.

A permanent return to Italy could also benefit coach Roberto Mancini, who – after the Under-21 European Championship (which Tresoldi will compete in with Germany) – would finally like him to play for the senior Azzurri side.

Nicolò, born in Cagliari in August 2004, is still free to choose which (senior) national team he wants to represent, and Mancini expressed his confidence earlier this week: “I spoke to Tresoldi, and Ranieri spoke to us too. First of all, I think he needs to feel the desire to play for Italy.

“He was born in Italy, like his father [former defender Emanuele], who played for the Under-21s and won the European Championship. I think there’s a chance he’ll choose the Azzurri. He knows he can be an important player for our future, and I hope he makes the right choice.”

#1778. Chelsea’s feisty friendly ends in penalty shoot-out confusion

Chelsea’s Far East tour ended in farce and confusion with players waiting around for a penalty shoot-out that never happened.

The chaos came at the end of a hard-earned, bad-tempered draw against Malaysian champions Johor Darul Ta’zim, with an own-goal in the 89th minute sparring the west London side’s blushes.

That goal also was supposed to set up penalties. But after minutes of waiting around – and Kevin Campello, Chelsea’s head of first-team operations, saying “it’s written in the contract” – the players walked off the pitch.

That confusion ended a feisty affair in which tensions threatened to boil over and that, at certain points, paid little attention to the “friendly” aspect of the clash with seven yellow cards shown. At one point the visitors’ new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee exchanged angry words with some of Johor’s coaching staff. The CFC TV commentary team suggested that the spot-kicks were abandoned because of the match’s heated atmosphere.

Austin MacPhee was ready to throw hands😂 pic.twitter.com/CFDgTOwmxE

Having played just 24 hours earlier in Jakarta – a 3-0 win over AC Milan – it was no surprise to see Xabi Alonso name a fresh XI, a mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters given much-needed game time.

And considering Johor are one game away from setting a new world record of 109 matches unbeaten in the top flight – a run that would surpass the current mark set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s – it was also no shock to see the Malaysian team offer a stern, pre-season test for the west Londoners.

After a good start Chelsea were second best in a first half in which Johor should have been at least two goals to the good. The Malaysian champions controlled the first 45 minutes and were 1-0 up after 14 minutes – a low cross from the left side-footed home by Arif Aiman.

The hosts gave the young, inexperienced Chelsea backline a torrid time, especially on the flanks and Óscar Arribas was guilty of not capitalising on a great chance to double Johor’s lead, his shot after cutting in from the right going wide.

While they looked vulnerable at the back, Chelsea also struggled to keep possession in attack. But they got an equaliser they scarcely deserved after Liam Delap was manhandled to the ground in the box by Kevin Medina. The striker, who may well leave Stamford Bridge before the transfer window slams shut, fired home the spot-kick allowing the visitors to go into the break on level terms.

For the most part, the second half followed a similar pattern to the first – Jofor having the better chances, while tensions on the pitch continued to run high.

It was, however, Chelsea who took the lead after the break, Delap once again scoring from the spot, this time after Jamie Gittens was brought down in the area.

Johor, though, kept on creating, thanks in part to a fairly porous visitors’ backline, and levelled through a deflected Arribas free kick, before going 3-2 up thanks thanks to a well-taken Bérgson strike.

Had it stayed that way Chelsea could have had few complaints. But as the clock approached 90 minutes, the visitors had one last attack. Mykhailo Mudryk, just on as a substitute, delivered a cross from the left that Antonio Glauder could only steer into his own net. That was supposed to set up the penalty shoot-out that did not take place and the chance for one of the sides to claim a hollow victory.

Considering a raft of changes and that fact this was far from the first XI, it is hard to know what to make of this. But among the positive things Alonso could take from the game was the impressive form of Nicolas Jackson and good centre-forward play of Delap. The negative was, however, a poor defensive display.

Chelsea return to Stamford Bridge on Saturday for their last pre-season friendly, against Real Sociedad, before the Premier League season starts away at local rivals Fulham on August 24.

Johor Darul Ta’zim: Syihan Hazmi; Arribas, Israfilov (Carlos Akapo 82), Medina, Antonio Glauder, Silva (La’Vere Corbin-Ong 89); Arif Aiman, Petrovic, Méndez (Nené 78), Marcos Guilherme (Bérgson); Zahedi (Stoichkov 62). Substitutes: Abad, Davies, Hidalgo, Nahuel Leiva, Lowry, Mohamadou Sumareh, Stuart Wilkin.Booked: Israfilov, Antonio Glauder, Silva.Goals: Arif Aiman (14), Arribas (65), Bérgson (86).Chelsea: Sharman-Lowe (Slolina 46); Subuloye, Adarabioyo, Anselmino (Watson 29); Geovany Quenda, Dario Essugo, Nicoll-Jazuli, Gittens (Mudryk 87); Estêvão, Delap, Jacskon (Satpaev 86). Good work from JDT who keep the ball well in midfield before a throughball is played to the on-rushing Zahedi but Slonina comes out well.

They’re back under way in Johor, and there’s an early chance for Jackson who gets the ball in the box, but the ball gets stuck underneath him and he cannot get in a good attempt in on goal.

And that is the last action of an entertaining half. Chelsea started well before the hosts opened the scoring. JDT then took control of the half and should, if truth be told, have extended their lead. But Delap did well to earn the penalty that he subsequently scored and should have made it 2-1 with the last kick of the 45.

Worrying signs at the back, however, for Alonso. Will Chelsea go to four at the back after the break?

The answer to that question (see last post) was so very nearly yes...

Jackson plays in a peach of a through ball with the outside of his right foot, Delap is one-on-one with the keeper and looks for all the world as though he has to score. BUT he scuffs his shot wide.

There will be three minutes of added time. Can Chelsea head into the break with an unexpected lead?

Free-kick for Chelsea on the JDT byline. The ball is put deep into the box, it’s headed back by Tosin before the ball is blazed over the bar.

A minute later Tosin then let’s fly form 25 yards, the ball goes well over the bar.

The hosts should have been more than 1-0 to the good and now they’re drawing. Goals change matches...

Having won the penalty Delap fires the spotkick home, sending the keeper the the wrong way.

Penalty to Chelsea and it’s all thanks to good centre-forward play by Delap. He gets the ball in the box and Medina manhands him to the ground. The referee doesn’t hesitate before pointing to the spot.

Chelsea have struggled to create anything since the opening 15 minutes. They have no control at the front and none at the back currently.

As I type that JDT have another good chance to turn the 1-0 lead into a 2-0 lead. Arribas, whose been a menace all game, dances toward the Chelsea box before delaying the pass too long.

JDT are finding a lot of joy on the flanks, there are three at the back for Chelsea and on the outside are two youngsters. The hosts are working the space well.

Yet again Chelsea are made to look decidedly average. A simple ball over the top on the right opens up the visitors’ defence and Arribas is in on goal, he cuts in and lets fly with his left peg, the shot going wide.

That should have been 2-0 to the Malaysian powerhouses.

Worrying signs for Chelsea who have struggled to keep possession up top and looked vulnerable at the back.

Yet more good work from JDT who are being given space by Chelsea. Marcos Guilherme slaloms into the west Londoners’ box and Tosin again doesn’t look the most assured but the JDT player cuts the ball back and the visitors can clear the danger.

Another good attack from the hosts who get in a shot in on goal, it’s deflected and loops into the grateful arms of Sharman-Lowe in the Chelsea goal.

There’s a break in play with Anselmino down and suffering what looks like a hamstring injury. He is eventually replaced by Reggie Watson.

Meanwhile, the home fans are in fine voice and waving several HUGE flags.

Yep, everyone’s least favourite part of the World Cup in the U, S of A is back. To be fair it’s humid in Johor so taking on fluids during the first 45 minutes is no bad idea.

There’s a bit of argy-bargy not really what you should get in a ‘friendly’. There hasn’t been a bad chellenge in the match so far so not sure where that came from...

Yet more good work from the hosts, this time it’s down the right, Arribas getting the better of Anselmino before shooting at the near post - the attempt hitting the side netting.

After a lively start Chelsea have been second best.

Poor defending from the visitors there but the chance was well snapped up by JDT.

Lovely break from the hosts. They break down the left at pace, before the ball is threaded through to the back post and Arif Aiman sidefoots into the back of the net with aplomb.

So very nearly an opener for Chelsea. They break at pace thanks to Estevao who drives down the middle before playing in Jackson. The striker cuts in from the left and shoots, the attempt is saved well by Hamzi and Estevao’s follow up is wide. Is a goal coming?

Free-kick for Chelsea some 35 yards out. Too far fro a shot on goal? Of course it is. The ball is floated into the box and the visitors earn a corner.

What can they create from this set piece? ‘Not much’ is the initial answer as the ball is cleared by JDT but Chelsea win possession back and the ball is fed to Estevao on the left, the Brazilian goes for go with his trusty left peg but the bal goes high and wide.

JDT attack down the left, it’s a lovely ball in that forces a fine header to clear the danger from Adarabioyo.

No sooner had I sent that last post than Chelsea break through the middle. The ball is fed through to Delap who gets a left-footed shot in on goal forcing a good save from the JDT keeper Hamzi.

Quiet, low-key start to the match. No real shock there, it is a pre-season friendly.

JDT give the ball away in their half and Chelsea have a half-decent platform to launch an attack from. They cannot fashion a chance and also lose possession.

They’re under way in southern Malaysia, Chelsea are in their vibrant blue and the hosts are wearing a fetching pink number. There was a late change for the visitors, Mamadou Sarr has been replaced by Olutayo Subuloye.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE JOHOR: Sharman-Lowe; Sarr, Tosin, Anselmino; Quenda, Nicoll-Jazuli, Essugo (c), Gittens; Estevao; Jackson, Delap; subs: Slonina, Curd, Subuloye, Diakite, Watson, Mudryk, Walsh, Kavuma-McQueen, Satpayev

...Luis Garcia. The Spaniard has history with Chelsea, remember the ‘ghost goal’?

Arriving for duty! 🫡 pic.twitter.com/M2XEkLC18n

Your Chelsea side today! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/0OvvGVmgpc

A mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters you may not have heard of.

Johor Darul Ta’Zim – more commonly known as JDT – are the Man Utd of Malaysia (at least that’s according to a Malaysian friend of mine). In 2013, they were going nowhere and were the dictionary definition of a stagnant club, low on confidence and trophies. That was until the Crown Prince bought the club and, over the next 13 years, transformed it into the powerhouse it is today.

As if to underline JDT’s dominance over Malaysian football they are one game away from the world record unbeaten run in a top flight. The new season of the Malaysian Super League gets under way later this month and should they avoid defeat in their opening match they will extend their unbeaten run - which began in April 2021 - to 109 games and surpass the world record set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s.

Chelsea’s pre-season tour of South East Asia ends today with a match against Johor Darul Ta’zim in Malaysia. The clash comes barely 24 hours after the west Londoners beat AC Milan 3-0 in Jakarta, a much-needed win coming on the back of defeats against Juventus and Tottenham.

A fine volley from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to victory in the Indonesian capital.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head into the break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

Alonso’s side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto.

Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Today, the west London side face Malaysian powerhouses Johor at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium, more on them later, but considering the tight turnaround from yesterday’s match today’s clash will provide a stern test.

“The idea, with the game against Milan and then one in Johor, was to arrive at this weekend with players not being ready for 90 minutes until now,” Alonso explained after the win in Jakarta.

“We wanted to have a logical progression in their loads; so we had our plan and we’ve stuck to that.

“We have another idea [against Johor]; that was decided yesterday [Friday]. The idea is that many young players were coming to have chances to play tomorrow. If not, we’d have been short, as playing two games in two days is quite intense. So we will need them.”

Stay here for all the team news and action with kick-off set for 1pm.

#1777. Cape Verde vs Liberia - prediction, team news, lineups

By Joshua Cole | 11 Nov 2026 18:45

Cape Verde will be looking to get their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying campaign off the mark when they welcome Liberia to the Estadio Nacional de Cabo Verde in Praia on Friday evening.

The Blue Sharks sit third in Group K after back-to-back defeats to Mali and Rwanda, while the visitors are bottom of the table and also without a point.

Cape Verde have made a disappointing start to the post-World Cup era, losing both of their opening Group K matches under new head coach Humberto Bettencourt.

They were beaten 3-1 by Mali before suffering a 2-1 home defeat to Rwanda, in which Gilson Benchimol's 40th-minute strike was cancelled out before half-time and the visitors scored again seven minutes into the second half.

Bettencourt, who spent six years as Bubista's assistant, has overseen two defeats in his first two competitive matches, leaving the Blue Sharks winless in their last six games (D3, L3), a run that includes goalless World Cup draws with Spain and Saudi Arabia, a 2-2 draw with Uruguay and a 3-2 round-of-32 defeat to Argentina.

However, their previous meetings with Liberia offer some encouragement, as Cape Verde have won three of the four encounters between the sides, including a 4-1 home victory in an Africa Cup of Nations qualifier in March 2011.

Liberia, meanwhile, began their qualifying campaign with a 3-1 defeat in Kigali, where Sylvanus Nimely scored their only goal before Rwanda restored their two-goal advantage from the penalty spot in the 44th minute.

The Lone Star then suffered a 1-0 home defeat to Mali, with Martial Tia's 79th-minute strike settling the contest.

Moroccan coach Mohammed Adil Erradi, who took charge of his first competitive match in Kigali, is still waiting for his first victory.

Liberia have won just one of their last eight matches (D2, L5), with that success coming in a 3-1 friendly victory over Sierra Leone in June, while they have scored just once in their two qualifiers, making a trip to Praia a difficult assignment for a side ranked 146th in the world.

Liberia Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:

Cape Verde have named a 26-man squad for the double-header, with goalkeeper Vozinha expected to start despite coming under scrutiny following the defeat to Rwanda.

The midfield options include Deroy Duarte, Kevin Pina, Jamiro Monteiro and Laros Duarte, while Dailon Livramento and Ryan Mendes are among the leading attacking options.

Huddersfield Town winger Derenseli Fernandes has been included, but defenders Roberto Lopes and Diney Borges are missing from the selection.

Liberia also have significant absentees, with captain Oscar Dorley ruled out after picking up a hamstring injury while playing for Saudi Arabian side Al-Taawoun.

Goalkeeper Tommy Songo is also injured, with Derrick Julu recalled to replace him.

Erradi has welcomed back Hammarby Talang striker William Gibson, while Ralph Weah has also earned a place in the 24-man squad.

Cape Verde have the quality and home advantage to make them favourites, although their defensive problems should give the visitors some encouragement.

The hosts should have enough to claim their first points of the campaign, but their recent struggles suggest it may not be a comfortable evening.

#1776. Forward line must step up to help deliver first Anfield win in 14 years

After a midweek journey to the north-west for the EFL Cup, we’re back in that neck of the woods today to face Liverpool in the Premier League.

The team news from the press conference was relatively promising, with Declan Rice, Riccardo Calafiori and Christos Tzolis all in training ahead of the game, and Mikel Arteta sounded relatively positive on Noni Madueke who missed out on the trip to Fleetwood Town. With Bukayo Saka out, and Max Dowman obviously suspended, he’ll start on the right and hopefully this run in the team will see him deliver a little more in terms of end product.

He got the backing of the manager beforehand, who said of him reaching his potential:

He has all the potential to do it, he has all the attributes to do it. He certainly has the will to do it because when you see him train every single day, he’s one of the players who enjoys the practice the most and wants to expose himself to all kinds of situations and actions. Now he needs to put the performance on the pitch.

Eberechi Eze should start on the other side, looking for his first Premier League goal contribution of the season, and I think the only other decision to be made is the construction of the midfield. Will it be Myles Lewis-Skelly or Bruno Guimaraes with Rice and Martin Odegaard? My own preference for a tricky away game is probably for Myles, because if you need to change something the Brazilian has attributes you can count on for that. However, he started him away in Munich, brought Lewis-Skelly on in his place when we were 2-1 down and that turned out all right. So, let’s see.

My guess is we’ll see: Raya, Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori, Rice, Guimaraes, Odegaard, Eze, Madueke, Havertz

After two goals in the first three games of the season, Kai Havertz has gone five without a goal in the Premier League, so today would be a good day for him to get back on track and to find some form again. I’d like to see him stay more central, to be something of a focal point rather than drift around the way he likes to. Perhaps when you face good centre-halves as he will today that’s part of how you disrupt them, but right now there’s real focus on our strikers and what they’re delivering (or not delivering as the case might be), and I hope that he, and Viktor Gyokeres when he gets a run later in the game, can produce what we need.

As for today’s opposition they’re still a bit of a work in progress under Andoni Iraola, but they seem to be getting to grips with what he wants. It took him a bit of time at Bournemouth, and the same seems to be true at Anfield, but Liverpool’s only defeat of the season was to Man City, collapsing late on after going down to 10 men. They have a couple of injuries, but in Alexander Isak they have a dangerous centre-forward in good form, and a player who has caused our central defenders plenty of problems in the past. Gabriel and Konsa will have to be at their best today, the sharpness of his movement in the box is really tricky to deal with.

It’s been 14 years since we last won away at Liverpool in the league, something Arteta views as a record to change:

It’s an opportunity. I came here and in many places we were 20, 22 years, 18 years without winning, and we’ve been doing all these things, so on Sunday, that’s the opportunity that we have.

Regardless of how you might feel about going out of the League Cup, you can be sure Mikel Arteta’s pride will have been hurt by both the defeat and the gleeful reaction to it in certain quarters. He will demand a response from his team today, and if that brings about a win at a ground that hasn’t been favourable for us in recent years, then you wouldn’t be at all surprised. Nevertheless, I think today will be a real test for two sides, neither of whom are in tip-top form right now, and two excellent coaches whose connection and friendship goes back years to add an extra dimension to proceedings.

Right, I’ll leave it there for this morning. As ever, we’ll bring you live blog coverage of the game later, as well all the post-game stuff on Arseblog News like the match report, player ratings, manager reaction, quotes round-up and more. There’s also a preview podcast on Patreon if you need something to listen to ahead of kick off. Don’t forget the updated Arseblog apps also have a cool new matchday centre, full of stats, alerts, and much more.

#1774. Liverpool 0-1 Arsenal: Resolute Gunners dig in for a big Anfield win

Fourteen years is a long time to wait for a win at any stadium, but Arsenal ensured all three points returned from Anfield to North London for the first time since 2012 yesterday.

The surprise in the team line-up was the return of Christos Tzolis who had missed a month, more or less, with a hamstring injury. If it initially felt a bit harsh on Eberechi Eze, Mikel Arteta’s post-game comments about him barely making the game because of an injury problem of his own made it make more sense.

Early on, we were really good. Plenty of the ball, playing it well in their half, and lots of control. Liverpool looked a bit off the pace, and in the opening minutes young midfielder Trey Nyoni was lucky to escape without some sanction for a nasty foul on Martin Odegaard. I think it was much more mistimed than malicious, but studs down the Achilles is never good, and we saw Crystal Palace striker Jean Philippe Mateta see red for something similar on Saturday evening.

The early pressure paid dividends when Liverpool were a little sloppy at the back. Odegaard pounced to recover the ball, it was fed to Noni Madueke via Bruno Guimaraes, and when Declan Rice overlapped, his precision ball to the back post found Kai Havertz for a tap-in to make it 1-0. That makes it 5 assists so far this season for the midfielder, all of them from open play as well, and his presence in this team reminds me so much of Patrick Vieira. Not that they’re the same kind of player, but that his importance and stature is just fundamental to us. The desire he showed with that overlap is, essentially, what cracked this game open in our favour.

There was another back post chance for Havertz, almost getting on the end of a deflected Guimaraes shot, but after that – as happens so often at Anfield – the momentum changed. This time there was no Granit Xhaka style confrontation to act as a catalyst, the game just shifted and in the final 20 minutes of the first half we rode our luck a bit.

Liverpool started to play around our box and deliver dangerous balls. One almost found Alexander Isak but a combination of David Raya and Ezri Konsa was enough to see it trickle wide. Florian Wirtz hit the bar with a free kick, and Liverpool wanted a penalty when Tzolis looked to pull back Cody Gakpo but I don’t think there was enough in that one. The next one, however, oooof.

Liverpool put in another dangerous cross, Isak was there to head towards goal from close range, and Jurrien Timber’s shirt pull absolutely prevented him from making contact with the ball. You know my rule of thumb with penalties: how would I feel it were given, or not given, up the other end, and if we didn’t get that I’d be fuming. It’s a penalty all day long, and even if the ref didn’t quite see the foul well enough, the VAR officials really ought to have suggested an on-field review. I found the focus on Isak’s reaction a bit odd. Surely the onus is on the officials to recognise what we’ve all seen without a player having to prompt them in that direction, but we got so, so lucky there.

As we did when Alexis Mac Allister ran into the box and, unmarked from 10 yards out, headed the ball over the bar when he absolutely should score. That was a very bad miss from a Liverpool perspective, and a huge chance to equalise just before the break. We needed half-time, and despite the fact Liverpool enjoyed plenty of the ball in the early part of the second period, they looked a lot less dangerous.

My explanation for this is that we leaned into one of our great strengths, which is our defensive organisation and discipline. I thought Konsa was outstanding, but so too was Riccardo Calafiori at left-back whose one on one defending has improved massively. He dealt with Gakpo, he then had to contend with Rio Ngumoha, and I just loved the concentration as he focused on the ball and more often than not prevented Liverpool from creating danger.

Myles Lewis-Skelly came on midfield, Odegaard’s pressing was relentless, and as I remarked on BlueSky afterwards, if this team could attack half as well as it can defend, we’d be the best team in the world by a mile. There were moments when we could have countered better and with more pace, but we still found some threat in the second 45. The best chance fell to Tzolis, set up by Madueke, and his first-time shot was heading for the bottom corner but for a brilliant save from Alisson.

Liverpool threw the kitchen sink at it from the bench, but it made little difference. Mac Allister then got a bit naughty, slapping Odegaard on the back of the head, then collapsing to the ground to make it look as if Madueke had leaned his head into him. Replays showed that didn’t happen, and it was pretty pathetic from the Argentina international. I guess, as well as being a risible piece of play-acting, there was an element of desperation to it, because Liverpool huffed and puffed but could not blow our house down because of how defensively outstanding we are as a team.

For the first time in Premier League history, Liverpool finished a home game without a shot on target, which tells you something. It probably tells you just how much that Timber shirt pull had an impact because a striker like Isak would at least have tested David Raya from there, but more broadly it tells you that this is a team who look laser-focused on their target this season which is to retain the title – something we’ve never done in the modern era.

Afterwards, I thought the manager’s turn of phrase was interesting when he referred to it as ‘a mission’, saying:

Just loving the mission and the mission was something that we didn’t accomplish in 14 years. You really need to enjoy that. If you don’t, there will be a moment that you will switch off and they will punish you. I think the way we competed and played and the chances that we generated as well, it was really impressive so I’m really happy.

He’s obviously referencing winning away at Liverpool for the first time in such a long time, but I think it applies to the season as well. And, as I referenced in yesterday’s blog, there was a response to the midweek defeat to Fleetwood Town. If that was a result that as fans we could find relatively easy to compartmentalise, I don’t think the same is true for this manager because we know he wants to win every game, and it how much it stings when we don’t – especially against lower league opposition. He expected his side to deliver, saying:

It was a feeling, how the hell can that happen? How can you get out of the cup when you shoot 27 times? We had the chances that we had against a team that had put one shot on target and then you look so silly. Then you have to go to Anfield and say, how can I lift those players up? I had a feeling and I said, now is the moment. We’re going to have to dig deep, have an element of luck at times and for sure a lot of quality in the key moments and we’ve done it.

Which I think is a pretty fair assessment. We did a lot of stuff very well, we had moments of luck – which you so often need in a game like this to take all three points – but I don’t think anyone should be under any illusions that this was anything other than the champions demonstrating our title credentials again. In every season, regardless of how good you are, you need the rub of the green from time to time, like a Ruud van Nistelrooy penalty miss at Old Trafford, or Mateus Fernandes missing a huge chance for West Ham. It doesn’t change the inherent quality you possess or what you’re capable of doing, and in the cold light of day it should make you more driven to ensure you widen the margins – and by that I mean delivering a bit more in the opposition’s final third.

However, no complaints this morning. We had a job to do, and a difficult one at that, and we did exactly that to put us back on top of the table. It’s a nice place to be, but it’s still so early in the season I think we should dismiss any chat about what it means at this point. We can be impressed, but still cognisant of the fact there’s still a long, long way to go.

Right, I’ll leave it there for now, but we will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on today. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

The pod should be out around around noon or so. Until then, have a good one.

#1773. MN: Why Milan and Inter are calm despite Council request over new stadium plan

A potential obstacle has already arisen after the Generali Stadium announcement, even if all parties remain calm for now.

As MilanNews recall, Tuesday morning’s edition of Corriere della Sera carried a report that had everyone on edge, just days after the renderings of the project were published. However, by the afternoon some quite important clarifications had arrived from Mayor Giuseppe Sala.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The newspaper reported that the Milan City Council had approved a bipartisan measure to halt the current environmental assessment process for the Generali Stadium project and request a new one that encompasses all the interventions the two clubs intend to undertake.

This includes the demolition of the current stadium once the new stadium is operational. The goal is to make the green light for the work conditional on a prior Health Impact Assessment (HIA).

MilanNews have learned that the City Council’s motion is non-binding, meaning Mayor Sala’s administration will not be obligated to follow the council’s request. More importantly, it does not suspend the Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA).

The two clubs remain calm regarding the next phases, especially since the SEA and the VIS are two separate and distinct phases that must both be addressed before work on the new stadium can begin.

The Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) is a procedure established by Italian and European legislation that evaluates the environmental sustainability of a plan or program prior to its approval.

It differs from the subsequent Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), which instead examines the environmental effects of a specific project prior to its potential authorisation and implementation.

The Council has therefore advanced a request that would not currently be foreseen under normal formal procedures. In any case, the two clubs are confident in the material produced, providing even more than necessary by integrating the Environmental Report with all the health-related details currently available.

Milan and Inter have no intention of avoiding any type of assessment. On the contrary, the EIA is scheduled for early 2027, by spring, with completion expected within a few months. Further investigations into the project and its impacts will therefore be undertaken shortly, as per the timetable.

Yesterday afternoon, Mayor Sala issues a statement on the news that broke, once again emphasising that the project will move forward.

“It’s clear that continuing to call the stadium issue into question is a gift to the right. I don’t want us to delude ourselves into thinking we’ve already won. I respect the City Council’s opinion, but the Council will respect the fact that I have no intention of reconsidering,” he said.

“We’ll discuss it in the City Council, but I have no intention of reconsidering the stadium. We’ve been talking about it for three years; everyone should do what they think best. I will continue to be consistent, and I will try to move forward with the stadium project.”

Councillor Martina Riva also gave a comment to MilanNews too: “Small obstacles? They won’t be a problem, we are convinced of the validity of our operation and we will move forward: the city, the teams and the fans who want a fully accessible stadium deserve it.

“I really like the Generali Stadium, it has exceeded all expectationsaccessibleI really like the Generali Stadium, it has exceeded all expectations.”

#1771. Morocco vs Niger - prediction, team news, lineups

By Joshua Cole | 11 Nov 2026 18:45

Morocco will be looking to maintain their perfect start to the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying campaign when they welcome Niger to the Mohammed V Stadium in Casablanca on Friday.

The Atlas Lions have collected six points from their opening two Group A matches and sit top of the table after beating Gabon and Lesotho, while the visitors are third with three points, having won one and lost one of their opening two qualifiers.

Morocco have made an impressive start to their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying campaign, winning both of their opening Group A matches against Gabon and Lesotho by identical 2-0 scorelines.

The Atlas Lions have scored four goals without conceding in the qualifiers, underlining their defensive organisation, while they have now kept clean sheets in three of their last four competitive matches.

Mohamed Ouahbi's side have since returned to action, playing out a 1-1 friendly draw with Mali in October, with Abdessamad Ezzalzouli scoring from the penalty spot in the first half before Gaoussou Diarra restored parity for the opposition.

The hosts will be looking to maintain their defensive solidity in competitive matches, and their previous meetings with Niger offer plenty of encouragement, having won all six encounters between the sides while conceding just once.

Morocco have also been particularly solid defensively in recent AFCON qualifying campaigns, conceding just twice in six matches during the previous edition of the competition and keeping four clean sheets, while they have now recorded six shutouts in their last eight matches in the tournament's qualifiers.

Niger, meanwhile, have struggled to build on their encouraging start to the qualifying campaign, opening with a 2-1 victory over Lesotho before suffering a 2-0 defeat against Gabon.

The Menas followed that loss with another 2-0 defeat, this time against Algeria in a friendly last month, leaving them with three losses from their last four matches across all competitions.

Their victory over Lesotho remains their only triumph in their last nine matches, a run that has also produced five defeats and three draws.

Niger's away record makes this an even more difficult assignment, with the Menas losing two of their last four competitive matches on the road, including a 5-0 defeat against Morocco in a previous World Cup qualifier.

Niger Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:

Morocco have several important absentees, with Ismael Saibari, Azzedine Ounahi, Ayoub El Kaabi, Soufiane Rahimi, Chadi Riad and Hamza Igamane all missing from the squad because of injury concerns.

Sofyan Amrabat, Amine Harit and Amine Adli are also absent from the selection, while Youssef En-Nesyri has returned to the national team and Ayoub Oufkir has received his first senior call-up.

Neil El Aynaoui has also withdrawn after suffering an ankle problem during the international gathering, with Samir El Mourabet called up as his replacement.

Niger have named a largely locally based squad for the double-header, with experienced players such as Oumar Sako, Ali Mohamed, Daniel Sosah and Tidjani Amadou Moutari included.

Nabil Neghiz has also made several notable omissions from his selection, including Hainikoye Abiboulaye and Amadou Wonkoye.

The visitors will likely attempt to defend deep and frustrate their opponents, but maintaining that approach for the full 90 minutes against Morocco's attacking options will be difficult.

The Atlas Lions have enough quality and depth to overcome a defensive setup and should create more than enough opportunities to secure a comfortable victory.

#1770. Fridges and pigs and scoring goals

We live in strange times. Sorry to start your day with this shocking revelation, I realise this is a bit of a bolt from the blue, but it’s fact. All across Europe supermarket fridges are being hacked. What a time to be alive. They used to hack, I dunno, mainframes and banks and shit, but now they’re hacking fridges.

Maybe they just got bored taking billions of made-up money from CryptoSloth and BitWomble and needed a challenge. I feel like fridges ought to be the kind of thing you just can’t hack – beyond unplugging it – but what do I know? Anyway, it’s an example of how the inter-connectivity that brings us all together every day is being weaponised and now the sliced meats in your local store are gone off because Neo pwned some large cold cupboards. As if we don’t have enough to deal with.

Such as all the people who hate the way Arsenal play. Let me be very clear, my days of caring what other people think about this football club, or pretty much anything else that’s important to me, are gone. It’s a waste of time. It’s a bit like quote that’s often attributed to George Bernard Shaw, which says ‘Never wrestle with pigs. You both get dirty and the pig likes it.’

I don’t think he actually said that, but I think we can all connect with the meaning. It applies so much to social media, and to many of the ways we’re exposed to punditry and ‘expert’ analysis in football these days. Like one of those shows where you have a couple of ex-pro pigs bleating on about this and that, and then a collection of other little pigs who support all the clubs argue with them and amongst themselves, and it’s just a pigstravaganza of pointless, inane bollocks but it does #numbers on socials so is seen as valuable #content.

I understand why opposition fans go on and on about how much they hate how Arsenal play. It’s because we win a lot of games. That’s the thing that really irks them. That’s just so basic though, you can’t appear to be clever and an aficionado of the game if you just say ‘I don’t like it when they win’, so it’s dressed up as dismissal of style or something else.

And look, here’s where the strange world we live in comes back into focus. You can, and really should, be able to hold more than one thought in your brain – about football or anything else – that holds true. I absolutely love how good we are defensively. LOVE IT. The commitment with which we are determined not to give the opposition anything is truly something to relish. Players laser-focused on their one on ones; putting bodies on the line to block shots and crosses; 11 players moving like a murmuration of birds because they’re so well drilled and organised; off the awareness and discipline; brilliantly timed tackles and headers and clearances; lads sticking up for each other when the opposition get a bit snide, as we saw on Sunday with Jurrien Timber and Noni Madueke refusing to allow their captain to be treated that way; it’s all part of a brilliantly defiant defensive attitude that runs right through this team.

Creating that is not easy. As Arsenal fans we have endured defences that were porous and feeble and, at times, very, very stupid. I do not long for a return to those times. Over the years Mikel Arteta has assembled a collection of players who cannot wait to go out there and do the dirty work of defending, and it runs from front to back because that’s what he demands. If it was that easy, everyone would do it, so to castigate a team’s brilliance in one department because you just lost to them without a shot on target just comes across as sour grapes.

Here’s the other thought though. I’d really like us to be a bit better from an attacking perspective, and when I look at this team and what it’s capable of, there’s no question the forward line remains the area where you can see the room for improvement. We defend as well as we do because, more often than you or I might like, we have to – because we live through games of fine margins. A 1-0 to the Arsenal is part of our history, hard-wired into our supporter DNA (particularly if you’re of a particular vintage), but I can’t lie and wish there weren’t a few more 3-0s to the Arsenal.

I’m absolutely certain Mikel Arteta would like that too, and I think it’s a bit too easy to say that this is a team that plays precisely the football he wants it to play. He is, as we all understand, an arch pragmatist, so what we get is a team that leans into its strengths, as laid out above. He is characterised as a defensive coach, which I get, but a few seasons ago we found an attacking cocktail that drove a title challenge, and saw us score more goals that year than the Invincibles did when they won the league in 2004 (91 to 73).

I think he wants both. He wants that parsimony at the back and the firepower up front. Unfortunately, forward line recruitment is the most difficult part of transfer business, and while he as manager has a part to play in that, as a club our track record is quite poor in that regard. This summer’s window was a complete bust from an attacking perspective, not a good look when you’re pursuing players like Morgan Rogers, Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez. When you then let three forwards go and add just one, there are questions to be asked of the people in charge. Arteta among them, of course, but he’s not the one whose job it is to get the deals done.

It’s why there are so many conversations around January, and what we might do. We see other clubs recruit forwards who produce on a consistent basis, while ours too often struggle to find that end product. Is it our system? Would these players find it hard to get those goals for us? Reasonable questions, but the bottom line in my opinion is that we have A+ options at the back and in midfield, while in that front three we’re a bit C-. That’s where the room for improvement is, that’s where the recruitment needs to be better (certainly better than no recruitment at all), and that’s how the games we currently win by a single goal margin, often by virtue of our defensive strength, become a bit more routine.

Simplistic? Yes. Easier said than done? Quite probably. But necessary? Absolutely. Until then though, expect more defensive masterclasses, more pig wrestling, and perhaps someone could hack our own Swedish fridge into scoring a few more goals. Worth a try!

Right, I’ll leave it there for now. I just have a small favour to ask. Arseblog has been nominated for Best Fan Media (Fran Merida) in the 2026 FSA Awards. We’re trying to retain our title, so if you could take a moment to give us a vote that would be much appreciated. You can do that here – https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/fsa-awards-2026

#1769. Andoni Iraola: Liverpool cannot ‘sustain the level’ I want

Andoni Iraola has conceded that Liverpool cannot currently “sustain the level” he expects after his side squandered a two-goal lead for the second match in a row.

In the Spaniard’s first game at Anfield since becoming manager, Monaco fought back to win 3-2 by virtue of Paris Brunner’s late glancing header seven days on from Leeds United’s 4-2 victory in Chicago, emphasising Liverpool’s alarming lack of depth, particularly in defence.

“We played a good first half, especially a good 30 minutes. Right now we probably don’t have much more, in terms of the levels required to play like this. They deserved to turn around the game.

“We won the first two pre-season games, but the last two we cannot sustain the level we want for all of the game. As soon as we made some changes, players start to get tired and we cannot sustain that level. So, we have work to do.”

Alex on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/PT6AYrLxyz

Alisson, Virgil van Dijk and Cody Gakpo all made their first appearances and contributed to a lively first-half in which Iraola’s commitment to man-to-man marking and an intensive pressing structure were evident out of possession. With the ball in the first half they demonstrated the kind of slick passing that Bournemouth employed to carve opponents open on the counter-attack.

A nimble one-two between Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai allowed the Dutch midfielder to set up Alexander Isak to score with a shot from 16 yards and the most expensive player in English football history laid claim to the second, too, when he seemed to hook in a rebound from Lukas Hradecky’s save while lying in the six-yard box.

Later he would graciously acknowledge that he and Florian Wirtz had connected with the ball simultaneously and he was happy to yield the credit to his team-mate.

Our second goal of the game, scored by Wirtz… we think 🤔 pic.twitter.com/FUzA363Oxw

At that point it seemed that victory would be a cakewalk but just before half-time Aleksandr Golovin caught Van Dijk out with a feint and late swerve to the right, tripping over the Liverpool captain’s clumsy hack. Despite a heavy limp, Golovin hammered the penalty past Alisson’s dive to make it 2-1 at the break.

Iraola rationed his early changes at the start of the second half to two but Liverpool could not regain their rhythm and Mika Biereth capitalised on a Gravenberch error to score the equaliser after battling to be first to the rebound when Giorgi Mamardashvili saved his first effort, stroking his effort through Wataru Endo’s legs.

Cue five substitutions as soon as that goal had gone in and a raft more followed, killing the remaining half-hour of all momentum and cohesion. By the time Brunner exploited a dozy mix-up between Milos Kerkez and Federico Chiesa about whose responsibility he was at a corner to flash his header past Mamardashvili, only two of the 22 starters were still on the pitch.

Liverpool: Alisson (Mamardashvili 46), Tsimikas (Kerkez 59), Van Dijk (c) (Chambers 59), Ndukwe (Endo 46), Frimpong (Ramsay 75), Gravenberch (Nyoni 59), Gakpo (Ngumoha 59), Wirtz (McConnell 59), Koumas (Chiesa 75), Isak (Muñoz 59)Substitutes: Morrison, Davies.Goals: Isak (16), Wirtz (29)Monaco: Hradecky, Nazinho (Mawissa 75), Dier (c) (Kehrer 75), S Sané, Vanderson (Teze 46), Golovin (Idumbo 75), Cabral (Soubeir 75), Camara (Benzahra 64), Detourbet (Coulibaly 64), Biereth (Brunner 80), Abline (Konaté 64).Substitutes: Assab, Kohn, Lienard, Nibombe, Touré.  Goals: Golovin (44 pen), Biereth (56), Brunner (88)

They played well in the first half, as they did against Leeds, but lost all shape and structure in the second half to lose 3-2.

Yellow card for Konate for clattering into Endo late. That’s the last of the action.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 3 (Brunner)  Brilliant near-post glancing header from a devilishly whippy, dipping corner. Kerkez doing his best Rip van Winkle impression.

Diligent defensive work by Ngumoha stops Konate’s run down the outside left.

A final substitution, hopefully. Brunner replaces Biereth. Konate’s shot, a pearoller, is easily saved by Mamardashvili after A mix-up between Kerkez and Munoz.

As usual, the substitutions have killed the game. Watched Leeds vs RB Leipzig yesterday. They played two 60 minute matches which kept it more competitive for longer but still descended into a kickabout late on.

Mawissa, Kehrer, Idumbo and Soubeir have replaced Nazinho, Dier, Golovin and Cabral.

Monaco also made changes, four I think. Will catch up with then once they’re confirmed. Ramsey is into the game straight away tp stop Coulibaly’s shot.

Ramsay, Chiesa and Elliott are coming on for Szoboszlai, Frimpong and Koumas. Lovely applause for Elliott.

Konate sweeps a left-foot shot from the left of the box past the right post with Mamardashvili forced into a headlong dive. Liverpool have lost their defensive shape and intensity, allowing Monaco to punch holes through the lines with some direct running.

Nazinho gets round Frimpong down the Monaco left and cuts back the perfect pass to put it on a plate for Coulibaly who hammers a left-foot shot from the right of the D that Mamardashvili throws up his hands to block. That would have stung. Good save. A flag would have meant it wouldn’t have counted but even so Frimpong’s defensive work wasn’t good enough.

It’s been very scrappy since the changes but then Ngumoha pounces on to a loose ball, glides up the right and tries to play Koumas in behind the back four. Sadly, he overhits the pass which trickles out for a goal-kick. Cue an ovation and cries of ‘Rio! Rio!’

Three changes for Monaco with Detoubet, Abline and Camara departing for Benzhara, Coulibaly and Konaté.

Ngumoha has gone to the right wing and Koumas is playing through the middle as a false nine.

Liverpool make five changes with Gakpo, Van Dijk, Wirtz, Tsimikas and Isak departing while Munoz makes his ‘debut’ with Ngumoha, Nyoni, Chambers, McConell and Kerkez.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 2 (Biereth) Mistake by Gravenberch allows Golovin to play a pass into the left half of the box for Biereth. Monaco overplay at the edge of the box, Detourbet, Biereth and Abline playing ‘after you. Claud’, instead of shooting.

A slick, short passing move between Gravenberch, Wirtz and Isak ends with Isak on the deck in the box after Gravenberch’s step-over allowed the ball to run to him. Quiet start to the half. Biereth just pressed Mamardashvili but the keeper managed to sweep the ball away even though under more pressure than he would have expected.

Liverpool try to play out from the back with Mamardashvili spearing a straight pass to Gravenberch who tried to knock it round the corner for Endo but the ball skidded under his studs and out for a throw-in.
